newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia mid-year budget review.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australia mid-year budget review.

text.p: The Australian government released its mid-year review of the budget on Tuesday.
Treasurer Peter Costello said the underlying budget deficit for the 1996/97 fiscal year to June 30 was A$8.49 billion from the A$5.65 billion forecast in the August Budget.
GDP growth in year average terms was unrevised at 3.5 percent. Year average underlying inflation was revised down to 2.0 percent from the 2.75 percent forecast in August.
The unemployment rate forecast for the June quarter was upwardly revised to 8.5 percent from an original 8.25 percent.
A selection of economists immediate reactions to the data follows.
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"Many of the changes were as we had expected, but we were disappointed in the size of the revision to the budget deficit. We were expecting something closer to A$7 billion, so A$8.5 is a bit of a disappointment. From the bond market perspective you have to weigh that against the lower inflation figures, but I think the bond markets were fairly optimistic on inflation anyway. They will now be looking for the government to address it seriously in the May budget."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER AUSTRALIA:

"I don't think it is surprising, although the extent of the blowout certainly is quite large given that they have left the growth forecasts where they are. For the market that seems it is tempered a bit by the extent of the downward revision in underlying inflation. I don't think there is that much in it for interest rates in the sense that the lower inflation is probably already factored in and with growth at 3.5 percent I guess the scope for the Reserve Bank accelerating growth from here is not all that great."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"Most of the revisions were pretty much as expected. The only real surprise was the extent of the deterioration in the budget position. Part of that was coming from a shortfall in company tax collections. It shouldn't have much impact on the market. The downward revision of the CPI numbers should just keep hopes of the possibility of a rate cut alive. Today's document also very much sets the scene for some further fiscal consolidation in the next budget in May."
SAUL ESLAKE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ANZ BANKING GROUP:

"The revisions to the economic forecasts were broadly as we had expected them, albeit that the government's forecast for GDP growth and employment were above our (own) expectations ... If our forecasts are correct rather than theirs, then the deficit, particularly for 1997/98, will be higher than projected in this review, but it would appear that most of the slippage in 1996/97 is a combination of the shortfall of company tax revenues and the Senate's rejection of various budget measures and the impact of lower inflation on the revenue side as well."

"The fact that there wasn't a downward revision to growth forecasts and that there were upward forecasts for 97/98 and out years might get rid of some of the bullishness at the short end. I have always been in the camp that there would be less than an even chance of another rate cut and I am not going to change my view on that. I still think it is more in favour of no (on an interest rate cut) than another easing at this stage and I think the key in all these numbers that wants me to stay with that view is that they didn't revise the GDP forecast down for this year and they revised it up for next year."
